claims.text: A machine-learning framework trained on transferable features from binary alloys can accurately identify high-entropy alloys with exceptionally low phonon thermal conductivity.
Local chemical fluctuations and force-constant variations enhance phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys.
FeCoCrMnNi is representative of a random five-element high-entropy alloy.
Single-phase high-entropy alloys such as those similar to FeCoCrMnNi are entropy stabilized.
High-entropy alloys possess severe lattice distortion and random local atomic environments.
A transformation module can convert binary-alloy compositional and structural features into an expanded feature space that is applicable to high-entropy alloys.
Local chemical fluctuations and force-constant fluctuations caused by severe lattice distortion mediate increased phonon scattering.
The variability of random atomic environments in high-entropy alloys produces enhanced force-constant fluctuations.
Force-constant fluctuations scatter acoustic phonons.
Acoustic-phonon scattering in FeCoCrMnNi is stronger than in its constituent simple elements.
Strong phonon scattering arising from severe lattice distortion reduces lattice thermal conductivity in high-entropy materials.
Learning latent correlations from binary-alloy systems allows the proposed model to capture the conductivity mechanism better than traditional theoretical models.
The proposed model could reduce phonon-thermal-conductivity prediction error by approximately 20% relative to conventional models.
High-entropy alloys selected by the proposed model will exhibit reduced lattice thermal conductivity because of stronger phonon scattering.
Conventional Callaway-Debye or similar models do not fully incorporate local chemical disorder and force-constant fluctuations.
Failure to incorporate local chemical disorder and force-constant fluctuations makes conventional models less accurate for predicting high-entropy-alloy phonon thermal conductivity.
Increasing configurational entropy can stabilize single-phase high-entropy materials.
The predictive approach is applicable primarily to uniform, single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The approach may not apply to multiphase or compositionally segregated materials because phase boundaries or other scattering mechanisms can dominate thermal transport.

The approach is falsified if more than 70% of tested alloys deviate from its predicted lattice thermal conductivity by over 10%, or if it fails to predict the expected lower-conductivity trend relative to conventional models.
